When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous surah the proof of His oneness, and mentioned the foundation, which is the Gathering (al-hashr), and concluded the surah with them, He began in this surah with the explanation of prophethood, saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it.﴾ What is in His saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ and in His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah and elsewhere, except that here He said ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾, whereas earlier He said ﴿a guidance and a mercy for the good-doers﴾ [Luqman: 3], and in al-Baqarah He said ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. The reason is that when a person sees a book in another's possession, the soul first begins to seek what is in the book, so it says: "What is this book?" When it is told that it is jurisprudence or tafsir, it then says: "Whose composition is it?" One does not first say: "This book, whose composition is it?" and then ask: "What is it about?" Knowing this, He first said: "This book is guidance and mercy," and then said here: "It is the Book of Allah, the Exalted," and mentioned it with the phrase "Lord of the worlds," because the book of One who is Lord of the worlds contains the wonders of the worlds, so the soul is drawn to study it.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, it is the truth from your Lord, that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, that they may be guided.﴾
That is: Do you acknowledge it, or do you say it is fabricated? Then He answered and clarified that the truth is that it is the truth from His Lord. Then He explained the benefit of the revelation, which is warning, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: How did He say ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come﴾ when the warners had preceded him?

The answer is in two respects: one is rational, and the other is transmitted.

As for the transmitted: the Quraysh were an unlettered people, and no warner had come to them before Muhammad ﷺ. This is

Page 146
far-fetched, for they were from the descendants of Ibrahim, and all the prophets of the Children of Israel were from their paternal cousins. And how would Allah leave a people from the time of Adam until the time of Muhammad without religion or law? And if you say that no messenger had come to them specifically, that is, that generation, then this was not exclusive to the Arabs; rather, the People of the Book also, that generation had not been reached by a messenger, but the messengers came to their fathers. Likewise, the messengers came to the fathers of the Arabs. Moreover, most hold that the fathers of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, were disbelievers, and because the Prophet threatened them and their fathers with punishment, and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15].

As for the rational: Allah, exalted is He, has a custom that when the people of an age have wholly gone astray and no one remains among them to guide them, He shows kindness to His servants and sends a messenger. Then, if He wills to purify them by removing shirk and disbelief from their hearts, or if He wills to purify the face of the earth by destroying them, then the people of that age went astray after the messengers, and no messenger came to them before Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. So He said: ﴿that you may warn a people to whom there has come﴾, that is, after the misguidance that followed guidance, no warner had come to them.

The second issue: If someone said: specifying something by mention implies negation of what is other than it, so His saying ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come﴾ requires that his warning be restricted to those to whom no warner had come. But the People of the Book had been reached by a warner, so the Book would not have been sent down to the Messenger to warn the People of the Book, and he would not be a messenger to them. We say: this is invalid in several respects.

The first of them: specification does not necessarily imply negation of what is other than it.

The second: even if someone holds it, he agrees with others that if the specification has a cause other than negating what is other than it, it does not imply negation of what is other than it, and here that exists, for warning them was more fitting. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And warn your nearest kinsfolk﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214], and it was not understood from it that he does not warn others, or that he was not commanded to warn others? And warning the polytheists was more fitting, because their warning was with tawhid and the Gathering, whereas the People of the Book were only warned on account of their denial of the prophethood, so they were more deserving of mention, and the specification occurred for that reason.

The third: on what we have mentioned, what he mentioned is not refuted at all; for the People of the Book had gone astray, and no warner had come to them from before Muhammad after their misguidance, so it follows that he is a messenger to all on an equal footing. By this the goodness of what we have chosen becomes clear. And His saying ﴿that they may be guided﴾ means: you warn them while hoping for their guidance.

When He mentioned the Message, He explained what the Messenger is responsible for: calling to monotheism (tawhid) and establishing the proof. So He said: ﴿Allah who created the heavens and the earth﴾. "Allah" is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate (khabar) is "who created." The meaning is: Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth, and none created them except One. Therefore there is no god but One.

We have already mentioned that His saying ﴿in six days﴾ refers to six states from the viewpoint of observers. This is because the heavens, the earth, and what lies between them are three things, and each has an essence (dhat) and attributes (sifah). Considering His creation of the essence of the heavens is one state, considering His creation of their attributes is another, and likewise for the essence of the earth and its attributes, and for the essences of what lies between them and their attributes. Thus there are six things in six states. He mentioned "days" because when a person looks at creation, he sees it as an act (fi'l), and an act has time as its container (zarf). Days are the most well-known periods of time. Otherwise, before the heavens there was no night or day. This is like someone saying to another:

"Indeed, the day you were born in was a blessed day."

It is possible that the person was born at night, and the speech does not depart from its intended meaning, because what is intended is the time that is the container of his birth.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿then established Himself upon the Throne﴾. Know that the scholars' position on this verse and similar verses is of two kinds:

The first: to refrain from explaining its intended meaning.

The second: to engage in explaining it.

The first is safer and closer to wisdom. As for its being safer: whoever says, "I do not engage in explaining this, and I do not know its intended meaning," is in the position of one who speaks when speaking is not obligatory, or of one who knows nothing, and it is not obligatory for him to know it. This is because the fundamentals are three: tawhid, belief in resurrection (hashr), and acknowledgment of the messengers. Concerning resurrection, we all agree that knowing it is obligatory, but knowing its details, such as exactly when it will occur, is not obligatory. This is why He said at the end of the previous surah: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]. Likewise, it is obligatory to know His existence, His oneness, His possession of the attributes of majesty and the descriptions of perfection in summary, and His exaltation above the defects of contingency (imkan) and the attributes of deficiency. But it is not obligatory to know all of His attributes as they truly are. The attribute of "istiwa'" is among those whose knowledge is not obligatory. So whoever refrains from engaging with it has not abandoned any obligation. As for one who engages with it, he may err in it and believe the opposite of what is actually the case. The first, at worst, does not know. The second is close to falling into compound ignorance (jahl murakkab), and the absence of knowledge is like silence, whereas compound ignorance is like lying. No one doubts that silence is better than lying.

As for its being closer to wisdom: whoever studies a book composed by a person and writes a commentary on it, the commentator is inferior to the author. Apparently, he does not cover everything the author covered. This is why we often see someone raise objections against an earlier author, and then someone else comes to defend his words and says: "The author did not mean this, but rather meant such-and-such." If this is the situation with created books written on limited knowledge, then what is your opinion of the Mighty Book, in which is every wisdom? Could an ignorant person claim: "I know every secret in this book"? And how, when even a scholar who claimed, "I know every secret and every benefit contained in such-and-such book," would be criticized for that? So how about one who claims that he knows everything in the Book of Allah?!

Furthermore, no one may say that Allah has explained everything He revealed, because delaying explanation until the time of need is permissible. Perhaps the Qur'an contains things that no one needs except His Prophet, and He explained them to him alone and not to others. Once this is established, it is known that the Qur'an contains things that are not known. This is closer to that which is not known, because of the extreme ambiguity (tashabuh) found in it. However, this position has a condition: that one negates some of what he knows, definitively, as not being intended. This is because if someone says, "These are the days of so-and-so's menstrual period (qur')," it is understood that he does not mean these are the days of so-and-so's death, nor the days of so-and-so's travel. What is intended is restricted to purity or menstruation. Likewise here, it is understood that what is intended is not what would imply deficiency in His essence, since that is impossible. Sitting and spatial settling belong to that category. Therefore it is necessary to affirm definitively the negation of these, and to suspend judgment about what is permissible beyond that.

The second position is risky. Those who hold it are of two groups. One says the intended meaning is its apparent meaning, which is standing upright, or spatial settling. The other says the intended meaning is "istila'" (dominion or taking control). The first is pure ignorance, and the second may be ignorance. The first, besides being ignorance, is an innovation (bid'ah) and nearly disbelief (kufr). The second, though it is ignorance, does not lead to an innovation. This is like one who believes that Allah shows mercy to the disbelievers and punishes none of them: this is ignorance, innovation, and disbelief. But if one believes that He shows mercy to Zayd, a person whose state is concealed (mastur al-hal), this is not an innovation. At most, it is an belief that does not correspond to reality.

Among what has been said about it: the intended meaning is "He established His dominion," and the Throne is used to express dominion. It is said: "The king sat on the throne of the kingdom in such-and-such city," even if he has not entered it. This is like His saying: ﴿The Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], which means stinginess, even though they did not claim that a chain is literally on the hand of Allah. Had Allah intended that literal meaning, it would be a lie, and the speech of Allah is far above that. Then there is a further clarification for this: kings have ranks. One who rules a small city or a modest land does not usually sit on a throne the first time he sits down. But a sultan who rules vast lands and wide territories, with kings in his service, has a throne on which he sits, and in front of him a chair on which his vizier sits. The throne and chair are customarily found only at the height of a kingdom's grandeur. Since the King of the heavens and the earth is in the utmost grandeur, He expressed it with what in common usage indicates grandeur. Something that alerts you to this is His saying: ﴿We created﴾ [al-Insan: 2], ﴿We adorned﴾ [al-Saffat: 6], ﴿We are nearer﴾ [Qaf: 16], ﴿It is We who sent down﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. Does any Muslim suppose or doubt that the apparent meaning of these is plural in the sense of partners? Can he find any interpretation for it other than that the great one in common usage is not single, but has others with him? Likewise, the great king in common usage is only one who has a throne on which he settles. So this expression is used to indicate greatness.

What supports this is that a defeated, subdued, routed person is described as: "The earth became too narrow for him until no place remained for him." Does anyone suppose that they mean he has become placeless? How can a body be imagined without a place, especially for one who claims his god is in a place? How can a person leave place altogether? Just as it is said of a fleeing, subdued person that no place remains for him, even though place is necessary for him, it is said of the powerful, dominant One that He is "established" and has a throne, even though exaltation above place is obligatory for Him. Based on this, the word "then" (thumma) means that He created the heavens and the earth, and then the account is that He established Himself upon dominion. This is like one saying: "So-and-so honored me and bestowed favors upon me many times, and I relate things about him," and then says: "He did not know me, and I had not done for him anything that would deserve this reward." So we say: "Then" (thumma) is for the narration, not for the narrated events.

The other opinion: it has been said that "istawa" means "istawla" (to take control) over the Throne. "Istawa" has come to mean "istawla" both through transmission (naql) and through usage. As for transmission, it is widely mentioned in lexicon books, among them Diwan al-Adab and others from which transmission is considered reliable. As for usage, there is the saying of a poet:

"Bishr has taken control of Iraq,
without sword or spilled blood."

On this basis, "then" (thumma) has the meaning we mentioned. It is as if He said: "He created the heavens and the earth, and then there is something greater than that: He established Himself upon the Throne," for the Throne is greater than the Kursi, and the Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth.

The third opinion: it has been said that the intended meaning is "istiqrar" (settling). This view is evident, and it does not indicate that He is in a place. This is because a person says, "So-and-so's opinion settled on going out," and no one doubts that he does not mean the opinion is in a place, which is going out, since an opinion cannot be described as occupying a place or as something that enters a place. Knowing this, we say: understanding "tamakkun" (being situated) when the word "istiqrar" is used is conditional on the possibility of tamakkun. So if someone says, "Zayd settled on the ship" or "on the couch," it is understood that he is situated and in a place. But if someone says, "Dominion settled upon so-and-so," it is not understood that dominion is in so-and-so.

Thus, the statement "Allah settled upon the Throne" should not be understood as meaning that He is in a place unless it is known that He is the kind of thing that can be in a place or cannot be. Therefore, understanding that He is in a place from this expression is conditional on the possibility that He is in a place. If the possibility of His being in a place were derived from this expression, it would require something to precede itself, which is impossible. Then, what shows that He cannot be upon the Throne in the sense of the Throne being a place for Him are several Qur'anic proofs:

First: His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ [al-Hajj: 64]. This requires that He be absolutely self-sufficient. Anything that is in a place requires a place to continue existing, because the immediate judgment of reason is that if the container (hayyiz) does not exist, the occupant (mutahayyiz) does not remain. So the occupant ceases when the container ceases. Whatever ceases when something else ceases requires that other thing to continue. Therefore, saying that He settles in a place requires that He need it for His continuance, while He is self-sufficient by the text.

Second: His saying: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The Throne will perish, and likewise every place will perish, while He remains. Thus at that time He will not be in a place. If it is permissible for Him not to be in a place, and what is permissible for Him of attributes is necessary for Him, then it is necessary that He not be in a place.

Third: His saying: ﴿And He is with you﴾ [al-Hadid: 4]. The argument from it is that "'ala" (upon), when used for a place, indicates that something is upon another in its essence, as when we say "So-and-so is upon the roof." And the word "ma'a" (with), when used of two who are situated, indicates their essential togetherness, as when we say "Zayd is with Amr." If Allah were in a place and we were situated, then His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with us﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40] and His saying: ﴿And He is with you﴾ should have meant togetherness, but that is not the case.

If it is said that "ma'a" is used to indicate that someone inclines toward another, or knows him, or supports him, as one says, "the king of such-and-such is with the king of such-and-such," meaning with aid and support, then we say: "'ala" is used to indicate that someone's authority is over another. If He is seen, He is seen in a place that encompasses Him, so visions perceive Him. As for when He is not in a place, then whether He is seen or not seen, it does not follow that visions perceive Him. As for when He is not seen, this is obvious. How is this, when the very thing this speaker clings to indicates that He is not upon the Throne in the sense of being in a place? The first: that place is eternal. Then this speaker claims to oppose the philosophers, yet he becomes a philosopher who says that one of the heavens is eternal.

The second: that movement and transition are permissible for God, the Exalted, and this leads either to the createdness (huduth) of the Creator or to the invalidation of the proofs of the createdness of bodies. And if there were no place, and what is in a place is one whose existence reason deems impossible without a place, then if it were permissible, it would not be possible to say that a body, if it were eternal, would either be at rest or in motion in eternity, because these two branch from being located in a place. Given this, it follows for him either to say that God is created, or not to say that the world is created. For if he concedes that before place He was not, then this is saying God is created, the Exalted. If he does not concede it, then it is possible that the body in eternity was not in a place, then came to be in a place, and then his proof for the createdness of the world is not complete, so it follows that he should not say it is created.

Furthermore, this speaker says: "You liken God to the non-existent, for He is not in a place, and you do not know that you have made Him non-existent by making Him in need of a place." Will you not then be mindful?﴾ When He mentioned that God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, some said: "We acknowledge that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is one, the God of the heavens. So God, the Exalted, said: There is no god other than God, no help from other than God, and no intercession except by God's permission. So your worship of them, these idols, is false and wasted; they are neither your creators, nor your helpers, nor your intercessors. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ of what you know, that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth. The creation of these great bodies cannot be done by idols like these, so that they could help you. And a great King would not have, toward these lowly things, reverence and magnificence such that they would have intercession.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count.﴾

When God, exalted is He, explained creation, He then explained command, as He said: ﴿Surely to Him belong the creation and the command.﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] Greatness is made manifest through both. Whoever possesses many great slaves has greatness, and when his command is effective among them, he grows in the eyes of the creatures. If his command is not effective, his greatness diminishes.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then it ascends to Him﴾, its meaning, and God knows best, is that His command descends from the heaven upon His servants, and their righteous deeds, which proceed in conformity with that command, ascend to Him, for the deed is the effect of the command.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾, there are several aspects to it.

The first: the descent of the command and the ascent of the deed cover a distance of a thousand years of what you count, while it occurs in one day. Between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years, so it descends over a journey of five hundred years and ascends over a journey of five hundred years, and this is the measure of a thousand years.

The second: this indicates the extent of the effectiveness of the command. Someone whose command is fully effective for one day or two days and then ceases is not like someone whose command is effective over long years. So His saying, ﴿in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years﴾, means ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ in a time, one day of which is a thousand years. How many months would be in it, how many years, and how many ages? In this respect, there is no difference between this and His saying: ﴿its measure is fifty thousand years﴾, because if that indicates the permanence of the effectiveness of the command, then whether it is expressed as a thousand or as fifty thousand makes no difference, except that the emphasis is greater with fifty thousand. We will explain its benefit in its place, God willing.

In this there is a subtle point: God mentioned in the preceding verse the world of bodies and creation, and indicated the greatness of the King. In this verse He mentioned the world of spirits and command by His saying: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾. The spirit is from the world of command, as He said: ﴿And they ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85]. He indicated its permanence with an expression that suggests time, while what is meant is the permanence of duration, as people say in common usage: "The time of so-and-so has lasted long." Time does not actually lengthen; rather, what occurs within time extends, so it exists across many times, and thus that lengthens and occupies many times. So He indicated there the greatness of the kingdom by place, and indicated its permanence here by time. Place belongs to His creation and dominion, and time is by His judgment and command.

Know that the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ in a Day suggests that His command occurs within a day, and a day has a beginning and an end, so His command would occur within a temporal duration, and thus it would be temporal (originated). Some who say that God is established upon the Throne say that His command is eternal, even the letters and the word "Be" (kun). So how is it understood from the word "upon" (ʿalā) that He is in a place, while it is not understood from the word "in" (fī) that His command is in a time?

Then He explained that this great King, whose command is effective, is not heedless. For a king who commands and forbids, and is obeyed in his command and prohibition, may be heedless and therefore not awe-inspiring and great. Whereas He is both aware and alert, and matters of the kingdoms and the subjects are not hidden from Him. So He said: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾.

Since He mentioned earlier the world of forms with His saying ﴿He created the heavens﴾, and the world of spirits with His saying ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾, He said: ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾, meaning He knows what is in the spirits, ﴿and the witnessed﴾, meaning He knows what is in the bodies. Or we may say: ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾ indicates what has not yet come into being, and ﴿the witnessed﴾ indicates what has been found and has existed. He placed knowledge of the unseen first because it is stronger and more indicative of the perfection of knowledge. Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. Having explained that He is All-Knowing, He mentioned that He is Mighty, capable of taking vengeance upon the disbelievers, and Merciful, of vast mercy toward the righteous.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who perfected everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay﴾. When He had explained the proof of His oneness from the horizons with His saying ﴿He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, and completed it with its consequences and complements, He mentioned the proof indicating it from the selves with His saying: ﴿Who perfected everything﴾, meaning He perfected everything of what He mentioned. He explained that what is between the heavens and the earth was created by Him, and it is as such. For when you look at things, you see them as they should be: the firmness of the earth for plants, the softness of the air for breathing, the receptiveness of the earth to being split for ease of passage, the flowing of water so that we can draw from it in every place, and the upward motion of fire, for if it moved like water, right and left, the world would burn. So it was created seeking the direction of above, where there is nothing that accepts burning.

As for His saying: ﴿and began the creation of man from clay﴾, it was said that what is meant is Adam, peace be upon him, for he was created from clay. It is also possible to say that clay is water and earth combined, and the human being's origin is semen, and semen's origin is nourishment, and nourishment is either animal or vegetable, and animal nourishment ultimately returns to vegetable, and plants come into being through water and earth, which is clay.

**[Page 151]**

The Most High said: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿Who made everything He created good, and began the creation of man from clay﴾ ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of a worthless fluid﴾.

* As for the Most High's words, ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of a worthless fluid﴾, according to the first interpretation (*tafsir*) it is clear, because Adam was from clay, and his offspring from an extract of a worthless fluid, which is the sperm-drop (*nutfah*). According to the second interpretation, its origin is from clay, and then from that origin there comes into being an offspring which is from a worthless fluid. If someone says: the second interpretation is not correct, because His words ﴿began the creation of man﴾ followed by ﴿then made his offspring﴾ indicate that the making of the offspring is after the creation of man from clay, we say: No, rather the second interpretation is closer to the verbal order, for He, exalted is He, began by mentioning the matter of the beginning of the creation of man, so He said: He began it from clay, then made it an offspring, then ﴿fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. According to what you have mentioned, it would be unlikely to say that ﴿then fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ also refers to Adam, because the word "then" (*thumma*) denotes sequence (*al-tarakhi*), so the fashioning would be after the making of the offspring from an extract, and that is after the creation of Adam. Know that the signs of the horizons (*al-afaq*) are more indicative of the perfection of power, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater﴾ (Ghafir 40:57), and the signs within the selves (*al-anfus*) are more indicative of the penetration of will, for the changes within them are numerous, and to this refers His saying: ﴿then made his offspring﴾, ﴿then fashioned him﴾, meaning: he was clay, so He made him a sperm-drop, then made him a human being, perfectly formed.

And the Most High's words: ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. The attribution of the spirit (*al-ruh*) to Himself is like the attribution of the House to Him, for honour. Know that the Christians fabricate lies against God and say that Jesus was the spirit of God, therefore he is a son. They do not know that every person's spirit is a spirit of God, by His words ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾, that is, the spirit which is His possession, just as a speaker says: "my house" and "my servant." He did not say "He gave him of His body," because nobility lies in the spirit. So He attributed the spirit and not the body, in accordance with what follows from the breathing of the spirit: hearing, sight, and knowledge. Thus the Most High said: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are the thanks you give﴾. Concerning this there are several questions:

**The first question:** He said ﴿made for you﴾, addressing them directly, whereas He had not addressed them before. This is because address is directed to a living being, so when He said ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ He addressed him afterwards, saying ﴿made for you﴾. If it is objected that address occurred before that, as in His words: ﴿And of His signs is that He created you from dust﴾ (al-Rum 30:20), we say: there He did not mention the ordered stages, but only indicated the completion of creation, whereas here He mentioned the ordered stages, which are the human being's being clay, then a worthless fluid, then a formed creature, equipped with various powers; so He addressed them at some stages and not at others.

**The second question:** The order in hearing, sight and hearts is according to the requirement of wisdom. This is because a person first hears things from his parents or from people and understands them; then as a result of that he acquires insight, so he sees matters and tests them; then as a result of that he attains complete perception and perfect intellect, so he derives things from his own faculty. An example of this: a person hears something from a teacher, then he becomes capable of studying books and understanding their meanings; then he becomes capable of composing, so he writes a book from his own heart. Likewise, the human being hears, then he studies the pages of existing things, then he knows the hidden matters.

**The third question:** He mentioned the verbal noun (*al-masdar*) for hearing, and the noun (*al-ism*) for sight and the heart; therefore He used the plural for sight and hearts, and did not use the plural for hearing, because the verbal noun is not pluralized. This is for a wisdom: hearing is one faculty with one function, for a person cannot retain two speeches at one time, and the ear is its locus with no choice in it, for sound reaches it from whatever direction it comes, and it has no power to specialize the faculty to perceiving some and not others. As for sight, its locus is the eye, and it has a semblance of choice, for it turns toward one visible object and not another. Likewise the heart is the locus of perception, and it has a kind of choice, turning toward what it wishes and not something else. Since this is so, the locus has no influence in hearing, and the faculty is self-sufficient; so He mentioned the faculty in relation to the ear, and in relation to the eye; and the heart has a kind of choice as a locus, so He mentioned the locus, because the act is ascribed to the one who chooses. Do you not see that you say: "Zayd heard and 'Amr saw," and you do not say: "the ear of Zayd heard" or "the eye of 'Amr saw," except rarely, for what we have explained, that the chooser is the origin and the others are its instruments. So hearing is the origin, not its locus, since it has no choice; the eye is like the origin, and the power of sight is its instrument; the heart is similar, and the power of understanding is its instrument. Thus for hearing He mentioned the verbal noun which is the faculty, and for sight and the hearts He mentioned the noun which is the locus of the faculty. Also, hearing has one faculty, and it has one function; therefore a person cannot hear two speeches at one time in a way that retains both, whereas he can perceive two or more images at one time and distinguish them.

**The fourth question:** Why did He put hearing first here, and the heart in His words: ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:7)? We say: this confirms what we have mentioned. In giving, He mentioned the lower and ascended to the higher, saying: He gave you hearing, then He gave you what is nobler than it, which is the heart. In taking away, He said: they have no heart with which they perceive, nor anything lower than it, which is the hearing with which they listen to one who has a heart that understands and derives realities. We have already mentioned there the reason for delaying sight, although it is in the middle in the order we mentioned: the heart and hearing were deprived of their faculty by nature, so He combined them, and He deprived sight of its power by placing a veil upon it, so He mentioned it later.

We have already mentioned there the reason for delaying sight, although it is in the middle in the order we mentioned: the heart and hearing were deprived of their faculty by nature, so He combined them, and He deprived sight of its power by placing a veil upon it, so He mentioned it later.

The Most High said: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿Who made everything He created good, and began the creation of man from clay﴾ ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of a worthless fluid﴾.

* As for the Most High's words, ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of a worthless fluid﴾, according to the first interpretation (*tafsir*) it is clear, because Adam was from clay, and his offspring from an extract of a worthless fluid, which is the sperm-drop (*nutfah*). According to the second interpretation, its origin is from clay, and then from that origin there comes into being an offspring which is from a worthless fluid. If someone says: the second interpretation is not correct, because His words ﴿began the creation of man﴾ followed by ﴿then made his offspring﴾ indicate that the making of the offspring is after the creation of man from clay, we say: No, rather the second interpretation is closer to the verbal order, for He, exalted is He, began by mentioning the matter of the beginning of the creation of man, so He said: He began it from clay, then made it an offspring, then ﴿fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. According to what you have mentioned, it would be unlikely to say that ﴿then fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ also refers to Adam, because the word "then" (*thumma*) denotes sequence (*al-tarakhi*), so the fashioning would be after the making of the offspring from an extract, and that is after the creation of Adam. Know that the signs of the horizons (*al-afaq*) are more indicative of the perfection of power, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Surely the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater﴾ (Ghafir 40:57), and the signs within the selves (*al-anfus*) are more indicative of the penetration of will, for the changes within them are numerous, and to this refers His saying: ﴿then made his offspring﴾, ﴿then fashioned him﴾, meaning: he was clay, so He made him a sperm-drop, then made him a human being, perfectly formed.

And the Most High's words: ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. The attribution of the spirit (*al-ruh*) to Himself is like the attribution of the House to Him, for honour. Know that the Christians fabricate lies against God and say that Jesus was the spirit of God, therefore he is a son. They do not know that every person's spirit is a spirit of God, by His words ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾, that is, the spirit which is His possession, just as a speaker says: "my house" and "my servant." He did not say "He gave him of His body," because nobility lies in the spirit. So He attributed the spirit and not the body, in accordance with what follows from the breathing of the spirit: hearing, sight, and knowledge. Thus the Most High said: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are the thanks you give﴾. Concerning this there are several questions:

**The first question:** He said ﴿made for you﴾, addressing them directly, whereas He had not addressed them before. This is because address is directed to a living being, so when He said ﴿and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ He addressed him afterwards, saying ﴿made for you﴾. If it is objected that address occurred before that, as in His words: ﴿And of His signs is that He created you from dust﴾ (al-Rum 30:20), we say: there He did not mention the ordered stages, but only indicated the completion of creation, whereas here He mentioned the ordered stages, which are the human being's being clay, then a worthless fluid, then a formed creature, equipped with various powers; so He addressed them at some stages and not at others.

**The second question:** The order in hearing, sight and hearts is according to the requirement of wisdom. This is because a person first hears things from his parents or from people and understands them; then as a result of that he acquires insight, so he sees matters and tests them; then as a result of that he attains complete perception and perfect intellect, so he derives things from his own faculty. An example of this: a person hears something from a teacher, then he becomes capable of studying books and understanding their meanings; then he becomes capable of composing, so he writes a book from his own heart. Likewise, the human being hears, then he studies the pages of existing things, then he knows the hidden matters.

**The third question:** He mentioned the verbal noun (*al-masdar*) for hearing, and the noun (*al-ism*) for sight and the heart; therefore He used the plural for sight and hearts, and did not use the plural for hearing, because the verbal noun is not pluralized. This is for a wisdom: hearing is one faculty with one function, for a person cannot retain two speeches at one time, and the ear is its locus with no choice in it, for sound reaches it from whatever direction it comes, and it has no power to specialize the faculty to perceiving some and not others. As for sight, its locus is the eye, and it has a semblance of choice, for it turns toward one visible object and not another. Likewise the heart is the locus of perception, and it has a kind of choice, turning toward what it wishes and not something else. Since this is so, the locus has no influence in hearing, and the faculty is self-sufficient; so He mentioned the faculty in relation to the ear, and in relation to the eye; and the heart has a kind of choice as a locus, so He mentioned the locus, because the act is ascribed to the one who chooses. Do you not see that you say: "Zayd heard and 'Amr saw," and you do not say: "the ear of Zayd heard" or "the eye of 'Amr saw," except rarely, for what we have explained, that the chooser is the origin and the others are its instruments. So hearing is the origin, not its locus, since it has no choice; the eye is like the origin, and the power of sight is its instrument; the heart is similar, and the power of understanding is its instrument. Thus for hearing He mentioned the verbal noun which is the faculty, and for sight and the hearts He mentioned the noun which is the locus of the faculty. Also, hearing has one faculty, and it has one function; therefore a person cannot hear two speeches at one time in a way that retains both, whereas he can perceive two or more images at one time and distinguish them.

**The fourth question:** Why did He put hearing first here, and the heart in His words: ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:7)? We say: this confirms what we have mentioned. In giving, He mentioned the lower and ascended to the higher, saying: He gave you hearing, then He gave you what is nobler than it, which is the heart. In taking away, He said: they have no heart with which they perceive, nor anything lower than it, which is the hearing with which they listen to one who has a heart that understands and derives realities. We have already mentioned there the reason for delaying sight, although it is in the middle in the order we mentioned: the heart and hearing were deprived of their faculty by nature, so He combined them, and He deprived sight of its power by placing a veil upon it, so He mentioned it later.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Rather, they disbelieve in the meeting with their Lord.﴾

When He said ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾, He showed their lack of gratitude by their bringing its opposite, which is disbelief and the denial of His power to give life to the dead. We have already mentioned that God, in His eternal speech, whenever He mentions two of the three fundamentals (al-usul al-thalatha, the three fundamentals of prophethood, monotheism and resurrection), does not omit the third. Here too, when He mentioned prophethood with His words ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ [al-Sajdah: 2] up to His words ﴿so that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3], and mentioned oneness (al-wahdaniyyah) with His words ﴿Allah is He who created﴾ [al-Sajdah: 4] up to His words ﴿and made for you hearing and sight﴾, He mentioned the third fundamental, which is the gathering (al-hashr, resurrection), with His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And they say, "When we have gone astray in the earth"﴾. There are several issues concerning this:

The first issue: the waw is for coordination (al-'atf) with what preceded from them. For they said, "Muhammad is not a messenger," and "God is not one," and they said, "The gathering is not possible."

The second issue: concerning their denial of the Messenger's prophethood, He said ﴿Or do they say﴾ in the present-tense form, and concerning their denial of him regarding the gathering, He said ﴿And they say﴾ in the past-tense form. That is because their denial of him regarding his prophethood did not occur before his existence; rather it occurred while he existed, so He said ﴿they say﴾, meaning they are in it. As for their denial of the gathering, it was earlier and issued from them and from their fathers, so He said ﴿And they say﴾.

The third issue: He explicitly mentioned their statement about prophethood where He said ﴿Or do they say﴾, and about the gathering where He said ﴿And they say, "When"﴾, but He did not explicitly mention their statement about oneness. That is because they were persistent in all circumstances in denying the gathering and the Messenger, whereas regarding oneness they acknowledged it in meaning. Do you not see that God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25]? He did not say, "They said that God is not one," even though they may have said it outwardly.

The fourth issue: If someone says: when He mentioned prophethood, He mentioned earlier its proof, which is the Book in which there is no doubt; and when He mentioned oneness, He mentioned its proof, which is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the creation of man from clay; but when He mentioned their denial of the gathering, He did not mention the proof. We say in reply: He did mention its proof as well, because the creation of man at the beginning is a proof of His power to restore him, [Page 154]
and for this reason God argued for the possibility of the gathering by the first creation, as He said: ﴿Then He repeats it, and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], and His words: ﴿Say, "He will give them life who brought them into being the first time"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 79]. Likewise the creation of the heavens, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81].

As for His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, meaning: shall we indeed be existing in a new creation, or be subjected to it? ﴿Rather, they disbelieve in the meeting with their Lord﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from the first statement; meaning, their denial is not merely of the bare act of creating them a second time, but rather they disbelieve in all the conditions of the Hereafter, even if they affirmed the creation a second time, since they acknowledged reward and punishment. Or we could say: its meaning is that they did not deny the resurrection in itself, but rather because of their disbelief; for they denied it, so they denied what leads to it. Then He explained what would befall them from death until the punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 32, verse 11:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been charged with you will take you back to your Lord.﴾

That is, death is inevitable, and after it there is life, and to this refers His words: ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾. His words "Then to your Lord you will be returned" are an indication that He does not neglect you, and when your term comes He does not delay you, since He has no occupation other than this. His words "The angel of death will take you back" indicate the survival of souls, for tawaffi (taking in full) is istifa' (receiving in full), and qabd (seizing) is akhdh (taking), while pure annihilation is not taking. Moreover, the pure and righteous soul remains with the angels like a person among his suitable relatives, while the wicked and corrupt soul remains with them like a captive among a people whom he does not know and whose language he does not understand. The former grows, increases, and its purity and strength expand, while the latter withers, weakens, and its wretchedness and turbidity increase. The philosophers say: pure souls become attached to a heavenly body better than their body and are perfected by it, while corrupt souls have no perfection after attachment.

The second point: if they mean by this what has been mentioned, then they agree with us; otherwise, the view must be examined according to what they intend. Their statement may be true or it may be untrue. If it is said: they denied resurrection, while God mentioned death, and between the two there is a clear opposition, we say: there are two aspects to this.

The first: that this (mention of death) is evidence for resurrection, and it removes the improbability of that. For they said: "When something has been wholly annihilated, how can the existing be that same thing?" So He said: the angel seizes the soul while the parts disperse, so gathering the parts is not far-fetched, and the command of the angel to return what he has seized is not difficult either. So His words "The angel of death will take you back" mean: the souls are known, and so they are returned to their bodies.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 32, verse 12:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿If only you could see when the guilty will hang their heads before their Lord, saying, "Our Lord, we have now seen and heard, so send us back; we will act righteously; indeed, we are now certain."﴾

When He mentioned that they would be returned to their Lord, He explained, in summary, what will happen at the time of the return, by His saying: ﴿If only you could see when the guilty hang their heads﴾, meaning: if you could see their condition and witness their shame, you would see a marvel. His saying ﴿you could see﴾ may be addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ) to comfort his heart, since they used to harm him with denial. It may also be general, addressed to everyone, as when one says: "So-and-so is generous; if you serve him even for a moment, he will be good to you for the rest of your life," and does not mean a specific person.

His saying ﴿before their Lord﴾ is to show the intensity of the shame, because when a servant has wronged his Lord and then stands before Him, he is in the utmost shame.
* * *
Then the Exalted said: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾, meaning they say, or are saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen﴾. He omitted "they say" to indicate the extremity of their shame, because one who is greatly ashamed does not speak. His saying ﴿we have seen and heard﴾ means: we have seen the gathering and heard the words of the Messenger, so send us back to the abode of the world that we may act righteously. Their saying ﴿indeed, we are now certain﴾ means: we have now believed. But what benefits is faith together with righteous deeds, and righteous deeds are only possible when one is charged with them, and that is in this world; so send us back to act. This is a falsehood on their part, for faith is not accepted in the Hereafter as righteous deeds are not. Or we may say that what is meant is that they deny association (shirk), as they said: ﴿By Allah, we were not polytheists﴾; so they say: what has befallen us has befallen us only because of abandoning righteous deeds, but as for faith, indeed we are certain, and we did not associate partners.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together."﴾ This is a reply to their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us [to the world]﴾. Its explanation is that He, exalted is He, said: "If I were to return you to faith, I would have guided you in the world. Since I did not guide you, it becomes clear that I neither willed nor wanted your faith, so I will not return you." His saying ﴿And had We willed, We would have given﴾ is explicit that our doctrine is correct, namely that we say: God did not will faith from the disbeliever, and did not will from him anything but disbelief. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell"﴾, meaning the word was fulfilled, which is His saying to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you﴾. This is with respect to transmission (naql), and it has a rational aspect (wajh fi al-'aql), namely that God, exalted is He, does not perform an act devoid of wisdom (hikmah). This is agreed upon. The disagreement is whether He intended the act for the sake of wisdom, or performed the act and wisdom necessarily followed from it, not in the sense that that wisdom compelled Him to the act? When it is known that His act is not free of wisdom, the philosophers (al-hukama') said: the wisdom of His acts, in its details, is not grasped in full detail, but it is grasped in summary. Every kind of occurrence in the world, and every corruption, has its wisdom emerging from a rational division: that an act is either pure good, or pure evil, or good mixed with evil. This last category is of three kinds: one kind whose good predominates, one kind whose evil predominates, and one kind whose good and evil are equal.

Once this is known: God created a world in which there is pure good, namely the world of the angels, which is the higher world (al-'alam al-'ulwi), and He created a world in which there is good and evil, which is our world, the lower world (al-'alam al-sufli). He did not create a world in which there is pure evil. Then, although good and evil both exist in the lower world, which is our world, it belongs to the first category, whose good predominates. For when you compare benefits with harms, and the beneficial with the harmful, you find the benefits more numerous; and when you compare the wicked with the good, you find the good more numerous. How could it be otherwise, when the believer is opposed by the disbeliever? Yet the believer may exist in such a way that there is no evil in him at all from the beginning of his life to its end, like the prophets, peace be upon them, and the saints. The disbeliever cannot exist in such a way that there is no good in him at all. The most that can be said is that disbelief nullifies his good and it does not benefit him. It is only deemed impossible, by the standard of custom, that there be a disbeliever who does not give a thirsty man a sip of water, nor feed a hungry man a morsel of bread, nor mention his Lord during his life. How could it not be so, when in his childhood he was created upon the natural disposition (fitrah) which inclines toward good?

Once this is established, we say: they say: were it not for evil in this world, God's creatures would be confined to pure good, and He would not have created the category in which good predominates and evil is little. Then, if the omission of creating this category is because of the evil in it, then forgoing much good for the sake of little evil is not fitting to wisdom. Do you not see that if a merchant is asked for a dirham in exchange for a dinar, and he refuses, saying: "In this there is evil, namely the departure of the dirham from my possession," it is said to him: "But in exchange for it there is much good, namely the dinar coming into your possession." Likewise, if a person abandons a slight exertion because of the hardship in it, while knowing that a lasting ease will result for him, he is held to be acting contrary to wisdom. So when one considers wisdom, the occurrence of much good mixed with little evil is a form of kindness (lutf), so He created the world in which evil occurs. To this He pointed with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am setting upon the earth a khalifah.﴾ They said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. God, exalted is He, replied to them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], meaning: I know that this category is consistent with wisdom, because the good in it is abundant. Then He made clear its good to them through teaching, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], meaning: O angels, the creation of pure evil, predominant evil, or equal evil is not consistent with wisdom. As for abundant good mixed with little evil, it is consistent. His saying ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] points to the evil, and God answered them with the good in it by His saying: ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾.

If someone says: God, exalted is He, is able to purify this category from evil so that no evil exists in it. It is said to him what God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾, meaning: had We willed, We would have purified the good from the evil. But then God would not have created the abundant good mixed with little evil, which is a rationally intelligible category. It would not have been permissible to forgo it because of the little evil, which is not consistent with wisdom, since forgoing abundant good for little evil is not fitting to wisdom. And if it were otherwise, there would be no obstacle to creating it, so He creates it for the abundant good in it. This is what those who hold that God observes what is best (ri'ayat al-maslahah) express: the good is in the decree (al-qada') and the evil is in the destiny (al-qadar); God decreed the good, and evil occurred in the destiny through His act, which is exalted above ugliness and ignorance.

His saying ﴿of the jinn and of men﴾: because He, exalted is He, said to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you﴾. This is an indication that the Fire is for those in the lower world, and those in the higher world are free of entering the Fire, and they are the angels. This requires that Iblis not be among the angels, and this is the correct view. His saying ﴿all together﴾ admits of two meanings.

The first: that it is an emphasis (ta'kid), and this is the apparent meaning.

The second: that it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning "gathered together."

If it is asked: how did He make all of the jinn and mankind the material with which Hell is filled? We say: this is to specify the category, meaning Hell is filled from the jinn and mankind and no others, as a safeguard for the angels. This does not require that all enter, just as one says: "I filled the bag with dirhams," which does not require that no dirham remain outside the bag. If it is said: this requires that Hell be narrow, filled with some of the creation. We say: that is so, and the one that is wide is only the Garden, which is of the wide mercy. And God knows best.

When God, exalted is He, made clear by His saying ﴿And had We willed, We would have given﴾ that they have no return, He said to them: since you know that you have no return.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 32, verse 14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your Day; indeed, We have forgotten you. And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do.﴾

The first issue: His saying, ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting﴾, may be in the accusative governed by "taste" (dhuqu), meaning: taste the meeting of your Day [i.e., its consequences] for what you forgot. In this case, what was forgotten may be the covenant that was taken from them by His saying, ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], or what is in the innate nature (fitrah) of monotheism, which is forgotten through turning toward the world and being preoccupied with it. It may also be in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿you forgot﴾, meaning: "for what you forgot of the meeting of this Day, taste." In this case, if someone says: "Forgetting occurs only regarding something previously known, when it has become unknown later," we say: when its proofs became manifest, it was as if it had appeared and become known; and when they abandoned it after its manifestation, it was mentioned with the word "forgetting," indicating that they were deniers of a manifest matter, like one who denies a matter he had known.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿this﴾ may carry three possibilities.

The first: that it refers to the Day, meaning: "So taste for your forgetting the meeting of this Day."

The second: that it refers to the meeting of the Day, meaning: "So taste for your forgetting this meeting."

The third: that it refers to the punishment, meaning: "So taste this punishment for your forgetting the meeting of your Day." Then He said: ﴿indeed, We have forgotten you﴾, meaning: We have abandoned you completely, not turning toward you, as the one who forgets does, to cut off your hope. Then He mentioned what necessarily follows from His abandoning them, as one who forgets abandons, namely the perpetuity of punishment, because whomever God does not deliver has no deliverance. So He said: ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do.﴾

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration and glorify the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant﴾. This is an indication that faith in the signs is like something already possessed, but some people forget it; so when they are reminded of them, they fall down prostrate to Him, meaning their limbs submit to Him, and they glorify Him with His praise, meaning they move their tongues in declaring Him far above association (shirk). ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾, meaning their hearts are humble and do not act proudly, and whoever is not arrogant about worshipping Him is the one who truly believes.

﴿Their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope, and from what We have provided them they spend﴾.

Meaning: by night they sleep but little. His saying ﴿they call upon their Lord﴾ means they pray (yusalluna), since supplication (du'a') and prayer (salah) are of one kind in meaning. Or it means they seek Him, and this does not contradict the first, because seeking may be done through prayer. Interpreting it as the first meaning is preferable, because He said after it: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾, and in most of the passages in which zakat is mentioned, prayer is mentioned before it, as in His saying: ﴿who establish prayer and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. His saying ﴿in fear and hope﴾ may be a verb of purpose (maf'ul lahu), or it may be a circumstantial state (hal), meaning fearful and hopeful, like your saying "they came to me as visitors (zuwwaran)," meaning visiting. It seems that the first verse indicates the highest rank, which is worship for the sake of God, exalted is He, while being oblivious to fear and hope, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿when they are reminded of them, they fall down﴾, for this indicates that at the mere remembrance, prostration arises from them even if there is no fear or hope. The second verse indicates the last two ranks, which is worship out of fear, like one who serves a mighty king out of dread of his wrath, or one who serves a generous king out of hope for his kindness. Then He explained what will be their reward for their deeds.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do﴾.

That is, [it is] of what the eye finds delight in and does not turn to anything else. It is said: "This does not enter into my eye," meaning my eye is not reaching out toward anything else. When the eye has no longing left for anything else, it has no room to look at anything besides it, so it is delighted, as a reward according to the ruling of the promise (bi-hukm al-wa'd). There is a subtle point (latifah) in this: from the servant there is something, which is righteous deeds, and from God there are things that came before, such as creation and provision and other things, and things that come after, such as reward and honor. Then, when He had threatened them, the Exalted said: ﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment, short of the greater punishment, so that they may return.﴾

That is, before the punishment of the Hereafter, We will make them taste the punishment of this world. The punishment of this world bears no comparison to the punishment of the Hereafter, because the punishment of this world cannot be severe and lasting. A severe punishment in this world destroys, so the one punished dies and is relieved of it, and it does not extend. And if the one punished wished for it to be prolonged, the punisher would not inflict on him a punishment of extreme severity. As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is both severe and lasting. There are two issues in the verse.

The first issue: the Exalted's saying ﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment﴾. Opposite it is "the farthest punishment" (al-'adhab al-aqsa), and opposite "the greater punishment" (al-'adhab al-akbar) is "the lesser punishment" (al-'adhab al-asghar). So what is the wisdom in pairing "nearer" with "greater"? We say: two things occur in the punishment of this world: one is that it is near, and the other is that it is small and minor. Two things also occur in the punishment of the Hereafter: one is that it is distant, and the other is that it is great and abundant. But nearness is the quality in the punishment of this world that is suitable for instilling fear, for a punishment that comes quickly, even if it is small, may be guarded against by some people more than a severe punishment that is delayed. Likewise, a quick reward may attract some people, and they consider a great delayed reward remote. As for the punishment of the Hereafter, what is suitable for instilling fear is its greatness and magnitude, not its remoteness, for the reason we have explained. So He said of the punishment of this world, ﴿the nearer punishment﴾, so that the sensible person would guard against it. Had He said "the lesser punishment," one would not guard against it because of its smallness and because one would not understand that it is imminent. And He said of the punishment of the Hereafter, ﴿the greater﴾, for that same reason. Had He said "short of the farthest, most remote punishment," the fear it instills would not have been like that produced by describing it as great. In sum, Allah the Exalted chose, for each of the two punishments, the attribute that is most suitable for instilling fear, over the other two attributes, for a profound wisdom.

The second issue: the Exalted's saying ﴿so that they may return﴾. "Laʿalla" (perhaps, so that) expresses hope (tarajji), and Allah the Exalted is far beyond that. So what is the wisdom in it? We say: there are two aspects.

The first: its meaning is "We will make them taste it in the manner of one who hopes," like His saying ﴿Indeed, We have forgotten you﴾, meaning "We have abandoned you," as one forgets someone and pays him no attention at all. Likewise here, We make them taste it in the manner of gradual treatment that is done to one who is hoped for.

The second: its meaning is "We make them taste the punishment in such a way that the speaker says: they may return because of it." We add another aspect from ourselves: every act that is followed by a desired outcome from that act may be explained by that outcome, as one says: "So-and-so traded in order to profit." If this explanation is in a case where the occurrence of the outcome from the act is not certain, considering the act itself, but certainty and knowledge arise based on something external, then it is correct to say: "He does such-and-such hoping for such-and-such," as one says, "He trades hoping to profit." If the trader has certainty of profit, this does not invalidate our saying "he hopes," since the certainty is not derived from the trade itself. But if the certainty arises from considering the act itself, it is not correct to say "he hopes," even if that certainty might admit its opposite. For example, if one says: "So-and-so cut his enemy's neck hoping that he would die," it is not correct, since certainty of death arises immediately after the cutting when considering the act, even though it is possible that he might not die, considering the power of Allah the Exalted.

What we have said is confirmed by the Exalted's saying about Abraham: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 82], although he knew of the forgiveness, but since certainty did not arise from the act itself, he applied the word "hope" to it. Likewise His saying: ﴿And hope for the Last Day﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 36], although certainty about it is necessary.

Having known what we have mentioned, we say: in every instance where Allah the Exalted said "la'allahum" (so that they), if we consider the act, certainty is not necessary, for from punishment it does not necessarily follow clearly that they will return. Thus our saying "He hopes" is correct, even if His knowledge of what will occur is complete. The utmost that can be said is that hope is used in most cases for something whose outcome is not known, which might give the impression that the term may not be applied to Allah the Exalted. That is not so; rather, hope (tarajji) is permissible with respect to Allah the Exalted, and it does not entail lack of knowledge; it entails only the absence of certainty based on that act, and the knowledge of Allah is not derived from the act. Thus the real meaning of hope is valid with respect to Him, in accordance with the sense we have mentioned.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Do they not see that We drive the water to the barren land, and bring forth thereby crops from which their livestock and they themselves eat? Will they not then see?﴾ ﴿And they say, "When will this victory be, if you are truthful?"﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that We drive the water to the barren land?﴾ When He had explained destruction, which is death, He explained revival, to indicate that harm and benefit are in the hand of God. The *jurur* (الجُرُزُ) is the barren land in which there is no vegetation. *Al-juruz* also means "cutting off," as though it is the land cut off from water and plants. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿and bring forth thereby crops from which their livestock and they themselves eat﴾. He placed the livestock before themselves in eating, for several reasons.

The first: crops, when they first sprout, are suitable for animals but not suitable for humans.

The second: crops are the food of animals, and it is indispensable. As for human food, it may come from animals. So it is as though the animal eats the crop, and then the human eats from the animal.

The third: an indication that eating is among the attributes of animals, and the human eats by his animality, or by the rational power within him. So his perfection lies in worship.

* * *
Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Will they not then see?﴾ Because the matter is seen, unlike the condition of the earlier generations, whose matters were only heard of. Then, when He had explained the messengership and the oneness of God (tawhid), He explained the gathering (hashr) by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "When will this victory be, if you are truthful?"﴾ to the end of the surah. Thus the arrangement of the end of the surah is like the arrangement of its beginning, where He mentioned messengership at its beginning by His saying: ﴿that you may warn a people﴾, and at its end by His saying: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾. He mentioned oneness (tawhid) by His saying: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-An'am: 1), and His saying: ﴿who made excellent everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay﴾. At the end of the surah He mentioned it by His saying: ﴿Has it not guided them﴾, and His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We drive﴾. He mentioned the gathering at its beginning by His saying: ﴿And they say, "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be [created] anew?"﴾, and at its end by His saying: ﴿And they say, "When will this victory be?"﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "On the Day of Victory, the disbelievers' faith will not benefit them, nor will they be reprieved."﴾ That is, their faith will not be accepted in that state, because accepted faith is that which occurs in the abode of this world. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾ means they will not be granted respite by being returned to the world so that they may believe and their faith be accepted. Then, when He had explained the matters and perfected the proofs, and it did not benefit them, He, exalted, said: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, do not debate with them after this; rather, the way after this is fighting.

His saying: ﴿and wait; indeed they are waiting﴾ admits of several meanings.

The first: wait for their destruction, for they are waiting for your destruction. On this reading, He distinguished between the two waitings: the Prophet's waiting (ﷺ) is by God's command after His promise, while their waiting is by the embellishment of their own souls and reliance upon Satan.

The second: wait for victory from God, for they are waiting for victory from their gods, and He distinguished between the two waitings.

The third: wait for their punishment on your own account, for they await it mockingly with their own words, as they said: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with﴾ (Al-A'raf: 70), and they said: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ (Yunus: 48), and other than that. And God knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final resort. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings upon the master of the messengers, Muhammad the Prophet, and upon his family and all his companions, and upon his pure wives, the Mothers of the Believers.

The first: wait for their destruction, for they are waiting for your destruction. On this reading, He distinguished between the two waitings: the Prophet's waiting (ﷺ) is by God's command after His promise, while their waiting is by the embellishment of their own souls and reliance upon Satan.

The second: wait for victory from God, for they are waiting for victory from their gods, and He distinguished between the two waitings.

The third: wait for their punishment on your own account, for they await it mockingly with their own words, as they said: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with﴾ (Al-A'raf: 70), and they said: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ (Yunus: 48), and other than that. And God knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final resort. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings upon the master of the messengers, Muhammad the Prophet, and upon his family and all his companions, and upon his pure wives, the Mothers of the Believers.
